'''Katherine Belov''' (born 1973) is an Australian [[geneticist]], professor of [[comparative genomics]] in the School of Life and Environmental Sciences and Pro Vice Chancellor of Global Engagement at the [[University of Sydney]]. She is head of the Australasian Wildlife Genomics Group and research expert in the area of comparative genomics and immunogenetics, including [[Tasmanian devils]] and koalas, two iconic Australian species that are threatened by disease processes. Throughout her career, she has disproved the idea that marsupial immune system is primitive, characterized the South American gray short-tailed opossum's immune genes, participated in the [[Platypus]] Genome Project, led research identifying the properties of platypus venom, and identified the cause of the spread of the Tasmanian devil's contagious cancer.

Belov is an advocate for [[Women in STEM]] and leads a research team of largely female students and post-doctoral students.

==Biography==
Katherine Belov was born in [[Sydney]], Australia in 1973 to Nick and Larissa Belov. Both of her parents were immigrants to Australia and of Russian heritage. Belov grew up in [[West Ryde, New South Wales]] and pursued her undergraduate degree at [[Macquarie University]] in human genetics. She was persuaded to change from human genetics to animal genetics by Professor [[Des Cooper]] who would become her PhD supervisor, and initially worked on [[grey kangaroo]]s, but quickly changed to the study of marsupials. She challenged a theory by another researcher who believed that marsupials did not have a highly developed [[immune system]] and proved that they had sophisticated immune systems comparable to our own. The research inspired her to enroll in a PhD program<ref name=bio>{{cite news|last1=Dow|first1=Steve|title=Saint among devils|url=http://www.stevedow.com.au/default.aspx?id=495|access-date=11 November 2015|publisher=Steve Dow Journalist|date=21 March 2010|location=Sydney, Australia}}</ref> on marsupial immunology at Macquarie University.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.abc.net.au/acedayjobs/cooljobs/profiles/s2599887.htm |title=Geneticist - Profiles - Cool Jobs - Ace Day Jobs |website=[[Australian Broadcasting Corporation]] |access-date=2015-11-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150612015220/http://www.abc.net.au/acedayjobs/cooljobs/profiles/s2599887.htm |archive-date=2015-06-12 }}</ref> She earned her PhD in 2002, and began her postdoctoral work at the [[Australian Museum]] with an [[Australian Research Council]] Fellowship.<ref name="PhD year">{{cite web|title=Us-Australian Academies Joint Workshop on Vertebrate Comparative Genomics|url=http://www.sciencearchive.org.au/events/conferences-and-workshops/genomics2007/belov.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151111144031/http://www.sciencearchive.org.au/events/conferences-and-workshops/genomics2007/belov.html|archive-date=11 November 2015|publisher=Australian Academy of Science|access-date=11 November 2015|location=Sydney, Australia|date=25 May 2007}}</ref>

In 2004, as part of the team, Belov became one of the primary researchers to sequence the genome of the [[platypus]]. The results, involving the work of over 100 international scientists, were published in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' in May 2008. Among the findings were that the platypus has unique [[anti-microbial peptides]] with broad-spectrum potential for fighting a variety of bacteria and viruses, and possibly [[staph infection]]s in humans.<ref name=bio /> Belov's research continued and she now leads her own team of researchers from the [[University of Sydney]], they began to characterise the platypus [[venom]], which has no antivenom and causes severe pain to humans. They were able to complete the analysis in 18 months, verifying seven snake-like zinc [[metalloproteinases]], seven toxins similar to the [[Latrotoxin|alpha-latrotoxins]] of [[Latrodectus|black widow spiders]], six [[cysteine-rich secretory proteins]] (CRISPs) like those found in some lizards and [[gila monster]]s, as well as some minor components similar to those of [[sea anemone]] venom.<ref name="anti-venom search">{{cite news|last1=O'Neill|first1=Graeme|title=Feature: Platypus venom spurs drug discovery|url=http://www.lifescientist.com.au/content/biotechnology/article/feature-platypus-venom-spurs-drug-discovery-906837014|access-date=11 November 2015|publisher=Life Scientist|date=19 July 2011|location=Wahroonga, Australia}}</ref>

In 2007, Belov accepted a lectureship position at the Faculty of Veterinary Science at the University of Sydney,<ref name="PhD year" /> after failing to secure a position elsewhere at the university, and began to focus on the [[Clonally transmissible cancer|contagious cancer]], [[devil facial tumour disease]], which started spreading through the Tasmanian devil population in 1996.<ref name="Tasmanian Devil Facial Tumour">{{cite news|last1=Ballance|first1=Alison|title=A Devilish Cancer - Tasmanian Devil Facial Tumour Disease|url=http://www.radionz.co.nz/national/programmes/ourchangingworld/audio/201753107/a-devilish-cancer-tasmanian-devil-facial-tumour-disease|access-date=11 November 2015|publisher=Radio New Zealand|date=5 May 2015|location=Wellington, New Zealand}}</ref> She worked with many others who proposed that the problem was that devils lack [[major histocompatibility complex]] gene diversity.<ref name=bio /> Belov proved her hypothesis, that devils do not mount an immune response to the cancer because the tumour's genetic makeup is so similar to their own.<ref name="no immunity">{{cite news|last1=Fessenden|first1=Marissa|title=Is Cancer Contagious? Could Hugo Chávez Have Been Deliberately Infected?|url=http://www.scientificamerican.com/article/is-cancer-contagious/|access-date=11 November 2015|publisher=Scientific American|date=18 March 2013|location=New York, NY}}</ref>

Belov became a full Professor of Comparative Genomics at the University of Sydney and has received an [[Australian Research Council]] (ARC) Future Fellow award to<ref name="The University of Adelaide">{{cite web|title=Guest Speaker - Professor Katherine Belov|url=https://www.adelaide.edu.au/environment/event/2013/kathybelov/|publisher=The University of Adelaide|access-date=11 November 2015|location=Adelaide, Australia|date=2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151118032635/https://www.adelaide.edu.au/environment/event/2013/kathybelov/|archive-date=18 November 2015}}</ref> continue her research in identifying genes, not only for devils and platypuses, but for other native Australian species like [[skinks]] and [[wallaby|wallabies]].<ref name="Cool Jobs">{{cite news|title=Cool Jobs Profile: Kathy Belov Age: 35|url=http://www.abc.net.au/acedayjobs/cooljobs/profiles/s2599887.htm|access-date=11 November 2015|publisher=Australian Broadcasting Corporation|date=2014|location=Sydney, Australia}}</ref> In 2014, she was awarded the [[Fenner Medal]] for research in biology from the [[Australian Academy of Science]].<ref name=medal>{{cite web|title=Awardees for 2014|url=https://www.science.org.au/awardees-2014|publisher=Australian Academy of Science|access-date=11 November 2015|location=Sydney, Australia|date=2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150709224424/https://www.science.org.au/awardees-2014|archive-date=9 July 2015}}</ref>

In 2016, she was appointed to the new role of Pro-Vice-Chancellor (Global Engagement) at the University of Sydney as part of its DEI initiatives.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://sydney.edu.au/news-opinion/news/2016/02/01/professor-katherine-belov-to-lead-global-engagement-strategy.html|title=Professor Katherine Belov to lead global engagement strategy|website=The University of Sydney}}</ref> This role includes responsibility for managing the development and execution of the University's global engagement strategy.

Belov's research team made some prominent discoveries in 2016. Firstly, new research that proved [[antimicrobial peptides]] (called [[cathelicidin]]s) in Tasmanian devil's milk can kill the deadliest bacteria and fungi, an important discovery in the fight against [[Antimicrobial resistance|superbug]]s.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Peel|first1=E.|last2=Cheng|first2=Y.|last3=Djordjevic|first3=J. T.|last4=Fox|first4=S.|last5=Sorrell|first5=T. C.|author-link5=Tania Sorrell|last6=Belov|first6=K.|date=11 October 2016|title=Cathelicidins in the Tasmanian devil (Sarcophilus harrisii)|journal=Scientific Reports|volume=6|issue=1|article-number=35019|doi=10.1038/srep35019|doi-access=free|pmc=5057115|pmid=27725697|bibcode=2016NatSR...635019P }}</ref> The second was the discovery of nine new genetic variants in the remote [[South West Wilderness|South West]] Tasmanian devil population.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.iflscience.com/plants-and-animals/not-devil-we-know-droppings-reveal-tasmanian-devil-diversity/|title=Droppings Reveal That Not All Tasmanian Devils Are Clones|website=iflscience.com|date=26 May 2016 }}</ref>

Belov has published over 170 peer-reviewed papers, mostly as passive author, including papers in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'', [[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]] and [[PLoS Biology]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://scholar.google.com.au/citations?user=bAdn-rEAAAAJ&hl=en&oi=sra|title=Katherine Belov - Google Scholar Citations|website=scholar.google.com.au}}</ref>

Now, her team, the Australasian Wildlife Genomics Group, studies the [[molecular genetics]] and evolution of gene families and [[genomes]] of our [[Fauna of Australia|native wildlife]].<ref name="auto">{{cite web|url=http://sydney.edu.au/vetscience/research/wildlifegenomics/index.shtml|title=Australasian Wildlife Genomics Group|first=Sydney School of Veterinary|last=Science|website=sydney.edu.au}}</ref> Research is focused on the immune system, evolutionary [[conservation genetics]] and applications for [[wildlife conservation|conservation]] management.

Belov promotes [[Women in STEM]] and sits on the [[University of Sydney]] SAGE Advisory Council.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://sydney.edu.au/about-us/vision-and-values/diversity/gender-equity.html#uniqueId_cefSjpFM_0_button|title=Gender equity in education|website=The University of Sydney}}</ref>

Belov received the Officer of the [[Order of Australia]] in recognition of her service as an academic and researcher to higher education (especially comparative genomics).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.smh.com.au/national/extraordinary-australians-honoured-in-annual-queen-s-birthday-ceremonies-20190606-p51v6q.html|title='Extraordinary' Australians honoured in annual Queen's Birthday ceremonies|last=Bungard|first=Matt|date=2019-06-09|website=The Sydney Morning Herald|language=en|access-date=2019-06-09}}</ref>

*2008 – The [[Australian Institute of Policy and Science]] (AIPS) Tall Poppy award<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.aips.net.au/tall-poppies/nsw-tall-poppies/past-nsw-tall-poppy-winners/2008-new-south-wales-award-winners/|title=2008 New South Wales Award Winners - AIPS|website=aips.net.au|access-date=2018-03-22|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190401234714/http://www.aips.net.au/tall-poppies/nsw-tall-poppies/past-nsw-tall-poppy-winners/2008-new-south-wales-award-winners/|archive-date=2019-04-01}}</ref>
*2009 – People's Choice Award, at the 20th [[Australian Museum]] [[Eureka Prizes|Eureka Awards]]<ref name="australianmuseum.net.au"/>
*2010 – ''Sydney Magazine'' Top 100 most influential Sydney-siders<ref>{{cite web|first1=The University of|last1=Sydney|access-date=2018-03-26|title=Professor Katherine Belov - The University of Sydney|url=http://sydney.edu.au/science/people/kathy.belov.php|website=sydney.edu.au}}</ref>
*2011 – [[Eureka Prizes|Eureka Awards]] Research and Innovation, Environmental Research, The Devils' Advocates<ref name="australianmuseum.net.au">{{cite web|access-date=2018-03-26|title=Past Winners & Finalists (Eureka Prizes) - Australian Museum|url=https://australianmuseum.net.au/eureka-past|website=australianmuseum.net.au}}</ref>
*2014 – The Genetics Society of Australasia "Ross Crozier Medal"<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.genetics.org.au/awards/|title=Awards » Genetics Society of AustralAsia|website=www.genetics.org.au}}</ref>
*2014 – [[Australian Academy of Science]], Fenner Medal for Research in Biology (Excluding the Biomedical Sciences)<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.science.org.au/past-winners/2014-awardees#fenner|title=2014 awardees - Australian Academy of Science|website=www.science.org.au}}</ref>
*2018 – Fellow of the [[Royal Society of New South Wales]]<ref>{{Cite periodical |date=31 January 2019 |periodical=Government Gazette of the State of New South Wales |url=https://gazette.legislation.nsw.gov.au/so/download.w3p?id=Gazette_2019_2019-8.pdf |title=Fellows |number=8 |access-date=13 November 2020 |archive-date=28 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201028192903/https://gazette.legislation.nsw.gov.au/so/download.w3p?id=Gazette_2019_2019-8.pdf }}</ref>
*2019 – [[Officer of the Order of Australia]]<ref name="ao">{{cite web |title=BELOV Katherine AO |url=https://honours.pmc.gov.au/honours/awards/2004470 |website=Australian Honours Search Facility |publisher=Australian Government |access-date=10 June 2019}}</ref>
*2022 – Fellow of the [[Australian Academy of Science]]<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-05-26 |title=Academy announces 2022 Fellows for outstanding contributions to science |url=https://www.science.org.au/news-and-events/news-and-media-releases/two-firsts-academy-announces-2022-fellows |access-date=2022-05-25 |website=Australian Academy of Science |language=en}}</ref>
*2024 – [[University of Glasgow]] Honorary Doctor of Science (DSc)<ref>{{Cite web |title=University of Glasgow Honorary Degrees 2024 |url=https://www.gla.ac.uk/news/headline_1058920_en.html |access-date=2024-07-24 |website=www.gla.ac.uk |language=en |archive-date=15 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240515193531/https://www.gla.ac.uk/news/headline_1058920_en.html }}</ref>
